title: Controller Area Network (CAN) Schedulability Analysis with FIFO Queues

extraction.paper_name: Controller Area Network (CAN) Schedulability Analysis with FIFO queues
extraction.paper_description: This paper extends CAN schedulability analysis to systems where some nodes use FIFO queues while others use priority queues. It introduces response time analysis for both priority-queued and FIFO-queued messages, considering the impact of FIFO buffering delays. It also derives optimal priority assignment policies for these mixed systems, demonstrating the detrimental effect of FIFO queues on real-time performance and bus utilization.

results.identifier: Transmission Deadline (E_m)

formal_description.statement: E_m = D_m - J_m

variables.E_m: Transmission deadline of message m (maximum permitted time from message being queued to reception)
variables.D_m: Hard deadline of message m (maximum permitted time from initiating event to successful transmission)
variables.J_m: Queuing jitter of message m (time from initiating event to message being in device driver queue)

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the effective deadline for a message once it is available in the device driver queue.

informal_sketch.intuition: The 'transmission deadline' is the actual time a message has to get from its queue onto the bus and be received, after accounting for any initial delays (jitter) from when its triggering event occurred.
steps: Identify the message's overall hard deadline (D_m).
Subtract the time it takes for the message to even reach the queue (J_m, queuing jitter).
The remaining time is the transmission deadline (E_m).
key_insights: Separates the total deadline into a pre-queue phase (jitter) and an in-queue/transmission phase (transmission deadline).
This is the deadline against which the response time from queuing is compared.

results.identifier: Worst-Case Response Time (R_m)

formal_description.statement: R_m = w_m + C_m

variables.R_m: Worst-case response time of message m (maximum possible transmission delay from queuing to reception)
variables.w_m: Maximum queuing delay of message m (longest time message m can remain in queue/buffers before transmission starts)
variables.C_m: Maximum transmission time of message m (time taken to transmit message m on the bus)

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total worst-case time a message spends from being queued until it is fully transmitted and received.

informal_sketch.intuition: The total time a message takes from being ready to transmit until it's actually sent and received is the sum of how long it waits in the queue and how long it takes to physically transmit.
steps: Calculate the maximum time a message waits in the queue (w_m).
Add the time it takes for the message to be transmitted on the bus (C_m).
This sum is the worst-case response time (R_m).
key_insights: Response time is composed of queuing delay and transmission duration.
This is the value compared against the transmission deadline to determine schedulability.

results.identifier: Message and System Schedulability

formal_description.statement: A message m is schedulable if R_m <= E_m. A system is schedulable if all messages in the system are schedulable.

variables.R_m: Worst-case response time of message m

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the condition for a message and an entire system to meet their real-time timing requirements.

informal_sketch.intuition: A message is considered 'on time' if its worst-case completion time (response time) is less than or equal to its allowed completion time (transmission deadline). If all messages are on time, the system is schedulable.
steps: For each message m, calculate its worst-case response time (R_m).
For each message m, calculate its transmission deadline (E_m).
If R_m is less than or equal to E_m for all messages, the system is schedulable.
key_insights: This is the ultimate goal of schedulability analysis: to guarantee that all messages meet their deadlines.
It links the calculated response times to the system's timing requirements.

results.identifier: Definition 1: Optimal Priority Assignment Policy

formal_description.statement: A priority assignment policy P is referred to as optimal with respect to a schedulability test S and a given network model, if and only if there is no set of messages that are compliant with the model that are deemed schedulable by test S using another priority assignment policy, that are not also deemed schedulable according to test S using policy P.

variables.network_model: A description of the system's characteristics and constraints

formal_description.conclusion: Defines what constitutes an 'optimal' priority assignment policy for a given schedulability test and system.

informal_sketch.intuition: An optimal priority assignment policy is the best possible one for a given schedulability test. If any other policy can make a system schedulable, the optimal policy can also make it schedulable (or better). It guarantees finding a schedulable assignment if one exists for that test.
steps: Consider a specific schedulability test (S) and network model.
A policy (P) is optimal if, for any set of messages, if they can be scheduled by *any* other policy (P') using test S, then they can *also* be scheduled by policy P using test S.
This means P is at least as good as any other policy in terms of finding schedulable systems.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_optimal_priority_policy(policy_P, sched_test_S, network_model):
    # This is a conceptual definition, not directly computable
    # It implies that policy_P is a 'supremum' in terms of schedulability
    # For any message_set:
    #   if exists policy_P_prime such that sched_test_S(message_set, policy_P_prime, network_model) is True:
    #       then sched_test_S(message_set, policy_P, network_model) must also be True
    pass
key_insights: Optimality is defined relative to a specific schedulability test, not absolute real-world schedulability.
An optimal policy maximizes the number of systems deemed schedulable by the test.

results.identifier: Definition 2: FIFO-adjacent priority ordering

formal_description.statement: A FIFO-adjacent priority ordering is any priority ordering whereby all of the messages sharing a FIFO queue are assigned adjacent priorities.

variables.FIFO_queue: A group of messages transmitted by the same FQ-node and sharing a FIFO queue
variables.priorities: The assigned priority levels for messages

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific structure for priority assignment where messages from the same FIFO queue occupy a contiguous block of priority levels.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a group of messages are all handled by the same FIFO queue, a 'FIFO-adjacent' priority ordering means that all these messages are given priorities that are next to each other, without any messages from other queues interleaved in between them.
steps: Identify all messages belonging to a specific FIFO queue (e.g., from ECU1).

Assign priorities to these messages such that their priority IDs form a continuous block (e.g., 100, 101, 102) and no other messages (from other ECUs or PQ-nodes) are assigned priorities within this block.
The internal ordering within this block can still vary (e.g., 100 could be the highest or lowest priority within the group).
key_insights: This ordering simplifies analysis by ensuring all messages from a FIFO group are treated as a single block for external interference.
It's shown to be beneficial for schedulability in mixed systems.

results.identifier: Definition 3: TDMPO-FP/FIFO (Transmission Deadline Monotonic Priority Ordering for FP/FIFO)

formal_description.statement: TDMPO-FP/FIFO is a priority assignment policy that assigns priority bands to priority queued messages and FIFO groups according to their transmission deadlines; with a shorter transmission deadline implying a higher priority. (Recall that the transmission deadline of a FIFO group is given by the shortest transmission deadline of any message in that group).

variables.FIFO_groups: Groups of messages transmitted by FQ-nodes
variables.transmission_deadline_m: Transmission deadline of a priority-queued message m
variables.transmission_deadline_group: Shortest transmission deadline among messages in a FIFO group

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific priority assignment policy that prioritizes messages/groups with shorter transmission deadlines.

informal_sketch.intuition: This policy assigns higher priorities to messages or entire FIFO groups that have tighter transmission deadlines. For a FIFO group, the deadline of its most urgent message dictates the group's priority.
steps: For each priority-queued message, determine its transmission deadline (E_m).
For each FIFO group, determine the minimum transmission deadline among all messages in that group.
Assign priorities such that entities (individual PQ-messages or entire FIFO groups) with shorter transmission deadlines receive higher priorities.
Within a FIFO group, messages are assigned adjacent priorities (as per Definition 2), but their internal ordering doesn't affect the group's overall priority band.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def assign_priorities_tdmpo_fp_fifo(message_set):
    entities = [] # List of (entity_id, deadline_value, type)
    for msg in message_set:
        if msg.is_priority_queued:
            entities.append((msg.id, msg.E, 'PQ_MSG'))
        else: # FIFO-queued
            # Assuming FIFO groups are pre-identified
            group_id = msg.fifo_group_id
            if group_id not in [e[0] for e in entities if e[2] == 'FIFO_GROUP']:
                min_group_E = min(m.E for m in message_set if m.fifo_group_id == group_id)
                entities.append((group_id, min_group_E, 'FIFO_GROUP'))
    
    # Sort entities by deadline (shorter deadline = higher priority)
    entities.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) # Sort by deadline value
    
    priority_map = {}
    current_priority = 1 # Highest priority
    for entity_id, deadline, entity_type in entities:
        if entity_type == 'PQ_MSG':
            priority_map[entity_id] = current_priority
            current_priority += 1
        else: # FIFO_GROUP
            # Assign adjacent priorities to messages within this group
            # (Internal ordering within group is not specified by TDMPO-FP/FIFO itself)
            messages_in_group = [m for m in message_set if m.fifo_group_id == entity_id]
            # For simplicity, assign internal priorities based on their own deadlines
            messages_in_group.sort(key=lambda m: m.E)
            for msg in messages_in_group:
                priority_map[msg.id] = current_priority
                current_priority += 1
    return priority_map
key_insights: This policy extends the well-known Deadline Monotonic Scheduling to mixed PQ/FQ systems.
It treats FIFO groups as single entities for priority assignment based on their most critical message's deadline.
It requires FIFO-adjacent priority ordering (Definition 2) to be effective.

results.identifier: Claim: Blocking Factor for PQ-nodes (B_m)

formal_description.statement: B_m = max_{k in lp(m)} (C_k)

variables.B_m: Maximum blocking time for message m due to lower priority messages
variables.lp_m: Set of messages with priorities lower than m
variables.C_k: Maximum transmission time of message k

assumptions: CAN message transmission is non-pre-emptable.
Fixed priority non-pre-emptive scheduling.
formal_description.conclusion: The maximum blocking time experienced by message m is the transmission time of the longest lower priority message.

informal_sketch.intuition: Since CAN messages cannot be interrupted once they start transmitting, a higher priority message (m) might have to wait if a lower priority message (k) has just started transmitting. The worst-case delay from this is the time it takes for the longest possible lower priority message to finish.
steps: Identify all messages (k) that have a lower priority than message m.
Find the maximum transmission time (C_k) among these lower priority messages.
This maximum C_k is the blocking factor B_m.
key_insights: This accounts for direct blocking in non-preemptive scheduling.
It's a fundamental component of response time analysis for CAN.

results.identifier: Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-nodes (w_m)

formal_description.statement: w_m = B_m + sum_{k in hp(m)} ceil((w_m + J_k) / T_k) * C_k

variables.w_m: Worst-case queuing delay of message m
variables.B_m: Maximum blocking time for message m
variables.hp_m: Set of messages with priorities higher than m
variables.C_k: Maximum transmission time of message k

assumptions: System comprises solely PQ-nodes.
Fixed priority non-pre-emptive scheduling.
Critical instant assumption (message m is queued simultaneously with all higher priority messages, which then re-arrive at their minimum periods).
formal_description.conclusion: This fixed-point iteration calculates an upper bound on the worst-case queuing delay for a priority-queued message in a system with only priority queues.

informal_sketch.intuition: The time a message (m) waits in the queue is determined by three factors: 1) initial blocking by a lower priority message already transmitting, 2) interference from higher priority messages that arrive and transmit before m, and 3) potentially push-through blocking from a previous instance of m. This formula iteratively calculates the total interference.
steps: Initialize w_m to a suitable value (e.g., C_m + B_m).
Iteratively calculate a new w_m using the formula:
The first term (B_m) is the blocking from lower priority messages (Claim: Blocking Factor for PQ-nodes).
The second term is the sum of interference from all higher priority messages (k).

For each higher priority message k, `ceil((w_m + J_k) / T_k)` gives the maximum number of times message k can arrive and interfere within the current busy period of length w_m, considering its jitter.
Each arrival of k contributes its transmission time C_k.
Repeat the iteration until w_m converges (i.e., the value no longer changes).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_w_m_pq_nodes(message_m, message_set):
    B_m = calculate_blocking_factor(message_m, message_set)
    w_m_current = message_m.C + B_m # Initial guess
    w_m_next = 0
    
    while True:
        interference = 0
        for message_k in message_set:
            if message_k.priority < message_m.priority: # Assuming lower number = higher priority
                num_arrivals = math.ceil((w_m_current + message_k.J) / message_k.T)
                interference += num_arrivals * message_k.C
        
        w_m_next = B_m + interference
        
        if w_m_next == w_m_current:
            break
        w_m_current = w_m_next
    return w_m_current
key_insights: This is a standard fixed-point iteration for response time analysis in non-preemptive systems.
It captures the cumulative effect of blocking and higher priority interference.
The `ceil` function accounts for all possible arrivals within the busy period.

results.identifier: Claim: Worst-Case Response Time for PQ-nodes (R_m)

formal_description.statement: R_m = w_m_plus_1 + C_m

variables.R_m: Worst-case response time of message m
variables.w_m_plus_1: Converged worst-case queuing delay of message m (from Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-nodes)
variables.C_m: Maximum transmission time of message m

assumptions: System comprises solely PQ-nodes.
Fixed priority non-pre-emptive scheduling.
formal_description.conclusion: The worst-case response time for a priority-queued message in a PQ-only system is its converged queuing delay plus its own transmission time.

informal_sketch.intuition: Once we know the maximum time a message has to wait in the queue (w_m), we just add its own transmission time to get the total time from queuing until it's fully sent.
steps: Calculate the converged worst-case queuing delay (w_m_plus_1) using the fixed-point iteration (Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-nodes).
Add the message's own transmission time (C_m) to w_m_plus_1.
The result is the worst-case response time (R_m).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_R_m_pq_nodes(message_m, message_set):
    w_m_converged = calculate_w_m_pq_nodes(message_m, message_set)
    R_m = w_m_converged + message_m.C
    return R_m
key_insights: This directly applies the definition of R_m (Definition: Worst-Case Response Time) after calculating w_m.
It's the final step in determining schedulability for PQ-only systems.

dependencies: Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-nodes (w_m)

results.identifier: Claim: Maximum Interference from Other Messages in Same FIFO Group (SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m)

formal_description.statement: SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m = sum_{j in M_m, j != m} C_j

variables.SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m: Maximum transmission time of all other messages in the same FIFO group as message m
variables.M_m: Set of all messages belonging to the same FIFO group as message m
variables.C_j: Maximum transmission time of message j

assumptions: FIFO-symmetric analysis (same worst-case response time attributed to all messages in a FIFO group).
In a schedulable system, at most one instance of each other message in M_m can be ahead of message m in the FIFO queue.
formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the maximum total transmission time of all other messages that could be ahead of message m in its FIFO queue.

informal_sketch.intuition: When a message (m) is put into a FIFO queue, other messages from the same queue might already be there. In the worst case, all other messages in that FIFO group could be ahead of 'm'. This sum represents the total time these 'ahead' messages would take to transmit.
steps: Identify all messages (j) that belong to the same FIFO group as message m, excluding message m itself.
Sum their maximum transmission times (C_j).
This sum is the maximum interference from within the same FIFO group.
key_insights: This term specifically accounts for the priority inversion caused by FIFO queuing within a node.
It's a worst-case assumption that all other messages in the group could be ahead.

results.identifier: Claim: Buffering Time for FIFO-queued Messages (f_m)

formal_description.statement: f_m = R_m - C_m

variables.f_m: Maximum buffering time for FIFO-queued message m (time from queuing until it becomes the oldest in its FIFO queue)
variables.R_m: Worst-case response time of message m
variables.C_m: Maximum transmission time of message m

assumptions: This definition applies specifically to FIFO-queued messages.
For priority-queued messages, f_m = 0.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the additional delay a FIFO-queued message experiences before it can even participate in bus arbitration, due to waiting in its FIFO queue.

informal_sketch.intuition: For a FIFO message, its 'buffering time' is the total time it spends waiting in its FIFO queue before it's even considered for bus arbitration. This is essentially its queuing delay (w_m) if we consider the response time (R_m) as queuing delay + transmission time (C_m).
steps: Calculate the worst-case response time (R_m) for a FIFO-queued message.
Subtract its own transmission time (C_m).
The remainder is the buffering time (f_m).
key_insights: This `f_m` term is crucial for modeling FIFO behavior as an 'increased jitter' for other messages.
It creates a circular dependency in the analysis, requiring iterative solutions.

results.identifier: Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-messages in Mixed Systems (w_m)

formal_description.statement: w_m = B_m + sum_{k in hp(m)} ceil((w_m + J_k + f_k) / T_k) * C_k

variables.w_m: Worst-case queuing delay of priority-queued message m
variables.B_m: Maximum blocking time for message m
variables.hp_m: Set of messages with priorities higher than m
variables.f_k: Buffering time of message k (0 for PQ-messages, calculated for FQ-messages)
variables.C_k: Maximum transmission time of message k

assumptions: System comprises both PQ-nodes and FQ-nodes.
Fixed priority non-pre-emptive scheduling.
Critical instant assumption.
The buffering time f_k for FIFO-queued messages is known (or iteratively determined).
formal_description.conclusion: This fixed-point iteration calculates an upper bound on the worst-case queuing delay for a priority-queued message in a system with mixed priority and FIFO queues, by treating FIFO delays as additional jitter.

informal_sketch.intuition: Similar to the PQ-only case, but now higher priority messages (k) might be FIFO-queued. If so, they experience an additional delay (f_k) before they can even start competing for the bus. This `f_k` is added to their jitter, effectively making them appear to arrive later from the perspective of bus arbitration.
steps: Initialize w_m to a suitable value (e.g., C_m + B_m).
Iteratively calculate a new w_m using the formula:
The first term (B_m) is the blocking from lower priority messages (Claim: Blocking Factor for PQ-nodes).
The second term is the sum of interference from all higher priority messages (k).
For each higher priority message k, `ceil((w_m + J_k + f_k) / T_k)` gives the maximum number of times message k can arrive and interfere. Note the addition of `f_k` to its effective arrival time.
Each arrival of k contributes its transmission time C_k.
Repeat the iteration until w_m converges.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_w_m_pq_mixed(message_m, message_set, f_values):
    B_m = calculate_blocking_factor(message_m, message_set)
    w_m_current = message_m.C + B_m # Initial guess
    w_m_next = 0
    
    while True:
        interference = 0
        for message_k in message_set:
            if message_k.priority < message_m.priority:
                # f_k is 0 for PQ messages, non-zero for FQ messages
                f_k_val = f_values.get(message_k.id, 0)
                num_arrivals = math.ceil((w_m_current + message_k.J + f_k_val) / message_k.T)
                interference += num_arrivals * message_k.C
        
        w_m_next = B_m + interference
        
        if w_m_next == w_m_current:
            break
        w_m_current = w_m_next
    return w_m_current
key_insights: This formula extends the standard response time analysis to account for FIFO queuing delays.
It models FIFO delays as an increase in effective jitter, allowing a unified interference calculation.
The `f_k` values introduce a circular dependency across messages, requiring an outer iteration (Algorithm 1).

dependencies: Claim: Buffering Time for FIFO-queued Messages (f_m)

results.identifier: Claim: Worst-Case Response Time for PQ-messages in Mixed Systems (R_m)

formal_description.statement: R_m = w_m_plus_1 + C_m

variables.R_m: Worst-case response time of priority-queued message m
variables.w_m_plus_1: Converged worst-case queuing delay of message m (from Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-messages in Mixed Systems)
variables.C_m: Maximum transmission time of message m

assumptions: System comprises both PQ-nodes and FQ-nodes.
Fixed priority non-pre-emptive scheduling.
formal_description.conclusion: The worst-case response time for a priority-queued message in a mixed system is its converged queuing delay plus its own transmission time.

informal_sketch.intuition: Once the maximum queuing delay (w_m) for a priority-queued message in a mixed system is determined, its total response time is simply that delay plus its own transmission time.
steps: Calculate the converged worst-case queuing delay (w_m_plus_1) using the fixed-point iteration (Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-messages in Mixed Systems).
Add the message's own transmission time (C_m) to w_m_plus_1.
The result is the worst-case response time (R_m).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_R_m_pq_mixed(message_m, message_set, f_values):
    w_m_converged = calculate_w_m_pq_mixed(message_m, message_set, f_values)
    R_m = w_m_converged + message_m.C
    return R_m
key_insights: This applies the definition of R_m (Definition: Worst-Case Response Time) to the queuing delay calculated for mixed systems.
It's the final step for determining schedulability of PQ-messages in mixed systems.

dependencies: Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-messages in Mixed Systems (w_m)

results.identifier: Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for FQ-messages in Mixed Systems (w_m)

formal_description.statement: w_m = B_m + SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m + sum_{k in hp(L_m) AND k not in M_m} ceil((w_m + J_k + f_k) / T_k) * C_k

variables.w_m: Worst-case queuing delay of FIFO-queued message m (arbitrary message from FIFO group M_m)
variables.B_m: Maximum blocking time for message m (from lower priority messages outside its FIFO group)
variables.SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m: Maximum transmission time of all other messages in the same FIFO group as m
variables.hp_L_m: Set of messages with priorities higher than the lowest priority message (L_m) in FIFO group M_m
variables.M_m: Set of all messages belonging to the same FIFO group as message m
variables.f_k: Buffering time of message k (0 for PQ-messages, calculated for FQ-messages)
variables.C_k: Maximum transmission time of message k

assumptions: System comprises both PQ-nodes and FQ-nodes.
FIFO-symmetric analysis (same worst-case response time attributed to all messages in a FIFO group).
Worst-case assumption: the arbitrary message m experiences interference as if it had the lowest priority (L_m) within its FIFO group.
The buffering time f_k for FIFO-queued messages is known (or iteratively determined).
formal_description.conclusion: This fixed-point iteration calculates an upper bound on the worst-case queuing delay for an arbitrary FIFO-queued message, accounting for internal FIFO blocking and external interference from higher priority messages (including their FIFO delays).

informal_sketch.intuition: For a FIFO-queued message, its queuing delay is a combination of: 1) initial blocking by a lower priority message, 2) waiting for other messages already in its own FIFO queue to transmit, and 3) interference from higher priority messages (from other nodes) that arrive and transmit. The analysis assumes the worst-case priority for the message within its group (lowest priority) to be pessimistic.
steps: Initialize w_m to a suitable value (e.g., C_m + B_m + SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m).
Iteratively calculate a new w_m using the formula:
The first term (B_m) is blocking from lower priority messages (Claim: Blocking Factor for PQ-nodes).
The second term (SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m) is interference from other messages within the same FIFO queue (Claim: Maximum Interference from Other Messages in Same FIFO Group).

The third term is the sum of interference from higher priority messages (k) *outside* its own FIFO group, considering their jitter and buffering times (f_k). The sum is over messages with priority higher than the lowest priority message in m's FIFO group (L_m).
Repeat the iteration until w_m converges.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_w_m_fq_mixed(message_m, message_set, f_values):
    B_m = calculate_blocking_factor(message_m, message_set) # B_m based on L_m's priority
    SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m = calculate_fifo_internal_interference(message_m, message_set)
    
    # Find L_m (lowest priority message in m's FIFO group)
    fifo_group_id = message_m.fifo_group_id
    messages_in_group = [msg for msg in message_set if msg.fifo_group_id == fifo_group_id]
    L_m_priority = max(msg.priority for msg in messages_in_group) # Assuming higher number = lower priority
    
    w_m_current = message_m.C + B_m + SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m # Initial guess
    w_m_next = 0
    
    while True:
        interference_external = 0
        for message_k in message_set:
            # k is higher priority than L_m AND k is not in m's FIFO group
            if message_k.priority < L_m_priority and message_k.fifo_group_id != fifo_group_id:
                f_k_val = f_values.get(message_k.id, 0)
                num_arrivals = math.ceil((w_m_current + message_k.J + f_k_val) / message_k.T)
                interference_external += num_arrivals * message_k.C
        
        w_m_next = B_m + SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m + interference_external
        
        if w_m_next == w_m_current:
            break
        w_m_current = w_m_next
    return w_m_current
key_insights: This formula combines external interference (from other nodes) with internal FIFO blocking.
The `hp(L_m)` term ensures that all messages that could possibly interfere with any message in the FIFO group are considered.
It's part of the iterative solution for `f_k` values across the system.

dependencies: Claim: Maximum Interference from Other Messages in Same FIFO Group (SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m)
Claim: Buffering Time for FIFO-queued Messages (f_m)

results.identifier: Claim: Algorithm 1 (Sufficient Schedulability Test with Arbitrary Priorities)

formal_description.statement:
Algorithm 1 iteratively computes the worst-case response times (R_m) and buffering times (f_m) for all messages until f_m values converge, then checks if R_m <= E_m for all messages. The algorithm is as follows:

Initialize all f_k = 0.
Repeat:
  Store previous f_k values as f_k_old.
  For each message m (in decreasing priority order):
    If m is PQ-queued:
      Calculate w_m using Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-messages in Mixed Systems (Eq. 5).
    Else (m is FQ-queued):
      Calculate w_m using Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for FQ-messages in Mixed Systems (Eq. 9).
    Calculate R_m = w_m + C_m.
    If m is FQ-queued:
      Calculate f_m = R_m - C_m.
Until all f_k values converge (f_k == f_k_old for all k).
Finally, for each message m, check if R_m <= E_m. If all pass, the system is schedulable.

variables.w_m: Worst-case queuing delay of message m
variables.R_m: Worst-case response time of message m

assumptions: The response times calculated via (5) & (6) and (8) & (9) are monotonically nondecreasing with respect to the buffering times (f_k).
The buffering times given by (10) are monotonically nondecreasing with respect to the response times calculated via (8) & (9).
This ensures convergence of the outer loop.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a sufficient schedulability test for systems with mixed PQ-nodes and FQ-nodes, handling arbitrary priority orderings by iteratively resolving circular dependencies between buffering times and response times.

informal_sketch.intuition: Because the buffering time (f_k) of a FIFO message depends on its response time, and its response time depends on the f_k of other messages, there's a circular dependency. This algorithm solves it by starting with zero buffering times, calculating response times, then updating buffering times, and repeating until all values stabilize. Once stable, it checks if all messages meet their deadlines.
steps: Initialize all FIFO buffering times (f_k) to zero.
Start an outer loop that continues until all f_k values stop changing:
Save the current f_k values.
For each message (typically in decreasing priority order):
If it's a priority-queued message, calculate its queuing delay (w_m) using the formula for PQ-messages in mixed systems (Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-messages in Mixed Systems).
If it's a FIFO-queued message, calculate its queuing delay (w_m) using the formula for FQ-messages in mixed systems (Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for FQ-messages in Mixed Systems).
Calculate its response time (R_m = w_m + C_m).
If it's a FIFO-queued message, update its buffering time (f_m = R_m - C_m).
Compare the newly calculated f_k values with the saved ones. If they are all the same, the loop terminates.
After convergence, for every message, check if its worst-case response time (R_m) is less than or equal to its transmission deadline (E_m). If all pass, the system is schedulable.
key_insights: This algorithm provides a practical way to perform schedulability analysis in complex mixed-queue systems.
The outer iteration handles the inter-dependencies between FIFO buffering times and message response times.
It's a sufficient test, meaning it might deem some schedulable systems unschedulable (pessimism).

results.identifier: Claim: Algorithm 1 (Simplified for FIFO-Adjacent Priorities)

formal_description.statement:
When a FIFO-adjacent priority ordering (Definition 2) is used, the buffering times f_k for all FIFO messages k can be set to 0. In this case, Algorithm 1 simplifies to a single pass over the priority levels (lines 11-14 of Algorithm 1 are omitted), using the following formulas:

For PQ-queued message m:
  w_m = B_m + sum_{k in hp(m)} ceil((w_m + J_k) / T_k) * C_k  (Eq. 5 with f_k=0)
  R_m = w_m + C_m

For FQ-queued message m:
  w_m = B_m + SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m + sum_{k in hp(L_m) AND k not in M_m} ceil((w_m + J_k) / T_k) * C_k (Eq. 9 with f_k=0)
  R_m = w_m + C_m

Finally, for each message m, check if R_m <= E_m. If all pass, the system is schedulable.

variables.f_k: Buffering time of message k (fixed to 0)
variables.w_m: Worst-case queuing delay of message m
variables.R_m: Worst-case response time of message m
variables.C_m: Maximum transmission time of message m

assumptions: A FIFO-adjacent priority ordering (Definition 2) is used.

This ordering ensures that any additional jitter on a FIFO message k due to other messages in its group is already accounted for by internal FIFO blocking, and not by external interference from messages of lower priority than k but higher than m.
formal_description.conclusion: This simplified version of Algorithm 1 provides a more efficient sufficient schedulability test for systems employing FIFO-adjacent priority orderings, as it eliminates the need for the outer iterative loop for f_k convergence.

informal_sketch.intuition: If all messages from a FIFO queue are grouped together in priority (FIFO-adjacent), then from the perspective of other messages, the FIFO group acts as a single, higher-priority entity. The internal FIFO delays are handled by the `SUM_C_other_in_FIFO_group_m` term, and there's no additional 'jitter' (f_k) that needs to be propagated iteratively. This means we can set all `f_k` to zero and perform a single pass.
steps: Assume all `f_k` values are 0.
For each message (typically in decreasing priority order):

If it's a priority-queued message, calculate its queuing delay (w_m) using the formula for PQ-messages in mixed systems (Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for PQ-messages in Mixed Systems), but with `f_k=0` for all `k`.

If it's a FIFO-queued message, calculate its queuing delay (w_m) using the formula for FQ-messages in mixed systems (Claim: Worst-Case Queuing Delay for FQ-messages in Mixed Systems), but with `f_k=0` for all `k`.
Calculate its response time (R_m = w_m + C_m).
After a single pass, for every message, check if its worst-case response time (R_m) is less than or equal to its transmission deadline (E_m). If all pass, the system is schedulable.
key_insights: This simplification significantly reduces computational complexity by removing the outer iterative loop.
It is valid only when FIFO-adjacent priority ordering is enforced.
It dominates the full Algorithm 1 in terms of efficiency for this specific priority ordering.

formal_description.statement: The schedulability of a message / FIFO group identified by m, may, according to test S, depend on any independent properties of other messages / FIFO groups in higher priority bands than m, but not on any properties of those messages / FIFO groups that depend on their relative priority ordering.

formal_description.conclusion: The interference from higher priority entities depends only on their presence and independent properties, not their specific ordering among themselves.

It's like saying 'how many people are ahead of me' matters, but 'who is first among them' doesn't affect my total wait time from their collective presence.

The interference term (summation) from higher priority messages (k) depends on the set of these messages and their properties (C_k, T_k, J_k, f_k).
The formula does not depend on the relative priority ordering *among* these higher priority messages.

formal_description.conclusion: The blocking from lower priority entities depends only on their presence and independent properties, not their specific ordering among themselves.

The blocking term (B_m) from lower priority messages (k) depends on the maximum C_k among them.
The formula does not depend on the relative priority ordering *among* these lower priority messages.

results.identifier: Claim: OPA Condition 3 (Priority swap effect)

formal_description.statement: When the priorities of any two adjacent priority bands are swapped, then the message / FIFO group being assigned the higher priority band cannot become unschedulable according to test S, if it was previously schedulable in the lower priority band. (As a corollary, the message / FIFO group being assigned the lower priority band cannot become schedulable according to test S, if it was previously unschedulable in the higher priority band).

variables.schedulability_test_S: The schedulability test being used (e.g., Algorithm 1 simplified)

assumptions: This condition applies to the schedulability test S (specifically, Algorithm 1 with lines 11-14 omitted).
formal_description.conclusion: Increasing the priority of a message/group cannot make it unschedulable, and decreasing its priority cannot make it schedulable, assuming other factors remain constant.

informal_sketch.intuition: If you give something a higher priority, it should logically have a better (or at least not worse) chance of meeting its deadline. This condition formalizes that intuition: improving a message's priority can't make it miss its deadline if it was previously schedulable, and worsening its priority can't make it meet its deadline if it was previously unschedulable.
steps: Consider two adjacent priority bands, one higher (H) and one lower (L).
Swap the messages/FIFO groups assigned to these bands.
The message/group moved to the higher priority band (H) should not become unschedulable if it was schedulable in the lower band (L).

This is because increasing priority reduces interference from other messages (by moving them to lower priority) and can only increase blocking (by moving a message to a higher priority than a previously blocking message), but the reduction in interference is always at least as large as any increase in blocking, leading to a non-increasing response time.
This condition holds for the simplified Algorithm 1 because increasing priority always leads to a non-increasing response time (as shown in the proof of Theorem 2).

It guarantees that the greedy assignment of priorities will lead to an optimal solution if one exists.

results.identifier: Theorem 1: FIFO-adjacent priority ordering optimality

formal_description.statement: If a priority ordering Q exists that is schedulable according to the FIFO-symmetric schedulability analysis of Algorithm 1 then a schedulable FIFO-adjacent priority ordering P also exists.

variables.Algorithm_1: The schedulability test (Claim: Algorithm 1 (Sufficient Schedulability Test with Arbitrary Priorities))

assumptions: The schedulability analysis is FIFO-symmetric (same worst-case response time for all messages in a FIFO group).
The response times and buffering times computed by Algorithm 1 are monotonically nondecreasing with respect to each other.
formal_description.conclusion: It is always possible to transform any schedulable priority ordering into a FIFO-adjacent one without losing schedulability, implying that FIFO-adjacent orderings are sufficient to find schedulable systems.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem says that if your system can be scheduled at all, you can always rearrange the priorities so that all messages from the same FIFO queue are grouped together (FIFO-adjacent) without making the system unschedulable. This simplifies the search for optimal priority assignments.
steps: Start with any schedulable priority ordering Q.
Consider a FIFO-queued message 'm' that is not the lowest priority in its FIFO group and has other messages (not from its group) interleaved between it and the lowest priority message of its group.
Shift 'm' down in priority so it's immediately above the lowest priority message in its FIFO group, effectively moving it closer to its FIFO group's block.

The proof shows that this transformation (to Q') does not increase the response time of 'm' or any other message, due to the monotonic relationship between buffering times and response times in Algorithm 1.
Repeat this process for all FIFO-queued messages until all FIFO groups have adjacent priorities, resulting in a FIFO-adjacent priority ordering P.
Since no response times increased, if Q was schedulable, P must also be schedulable.

results.identifier: Theorem 2: OPA-FP/FIFO optimality

formal_description.statement: The OPA-FP/FIFO algorithm is an optimal priority assignment algorithm with respect to the FIFO-symmetric schedulability test of section IV.E (Algorithm 1 with lines 11-14 omitted).

variables.OPA_FP_FIFO_algorithm: Audsley's Optimal Priority Assignment algorithm adapted for FP/FIFO systems

assumptions: The schedulability test (Algorithm 1 simplified) satisfies OPA Conditions 1, 2, and 3.
formal_description.conclusion: The OPA-FP/FIFO algorithm is guaranteed to find a schedulable priority assignment (if one exists) for the simplified schedulability test, making it an optimal priority assignment policy for this specific test.

informal_sketch.intuition: Audsley's Optimal Priority Assignment (OPA) algorithm is a powerful method for finding optimal priority assignments. This theorem states that if we adapt OPA to handle FIFO groups (OPA-FP/FIFO) and use the simplified schedulability test (which assumes FIFO-adjacent priorities), then this adapted OPA algorithm will find an optimal priority assignment.
steps: To prove OPA-FP/FIFO is optimal, one must show that the underlying schedulability test (Claim: Algorithm 1 (Simplified for FIFO-Adjacent Priorities)) satisfies three specific conditions (Claim: OPA Condition 1, Claim: OPA Condition 2, Claim: OPA Condition 3).

Condition 1 (dependence on higher priority independent properties): The interference term in the simplified formulas (Eq. 5 and 9 with f_k=0) depends on the *set* of higher priority messages/groups, not their internal ordering.
Condition 2 (dependence on lower priority independent properties): The blocking term (B_m) depends on the *set* of lower priority messages/groups, not their internal ordering.

Condition 3 (monotonicity of priority swaps): Increasing a message's priority (moving it to a higher band) cannot increase its response time, because any increase in blocking is offset by a larger or equal decrease in interference.
Since all three conditions hold, OPA-FP/FIFO is optimal for this specific schedulability test.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def prove_theorem_2(sched_test_S_simplified):
    # Conceptual proof sketch: show that sched_test_S_simplified satisfies OPA Conditions 1, 2, 3
    # (This is a conceptual proof, not executable code)
    if check_opa_condition_1(sched_test_S_simplified) and \
       check_opa_condition_2(sched_test_S_simplified) and \
       check_opa_condition_3(sched_test_S_simplified):
        return True # OPA-FP/FIFO is optimal
    return False
key_insights: This theorem provides a robust method for assigning priorities in mixed PQ/FQ systems under the FIFO-adjacent assumption.
It leverages the well-established theory of Audsley's OPA algorithm.
The proof relies on the specific structure and properties of the derived response time equations.
